title: What Should Kids Study in the Age of AI? The Answer Is Shifting Fast.
excerpt: As nearly half of college students rethink their majors because of AI, educators and employers are converging on a new set of skills: critical thinking, adaptability, and the ability to ask better questions.
body:
• A Gallup-Lumina study found 42% of bachelor's degree students have reconsidered their major because of AI, and 16% have already switched
  • Employers now prioritize critical thinking, communication, and AI literacy over specialized technical knowledge, according to multiple surveys
  • Faculty at American universities overwhelmingly worry that AI is eroding students' critical thinking (90%) and deepening overreliance on tools (95%)
  • Education experts argue that what makes humans irreplaceable — creativity, empathy, judgment — should become the core curriculum

A generation of students is entering the workforce in the middle of the most significant shift in how knowledge work gets done since the internet. And they know it.

According to a 2026 study by the Lumina Foundation and Gallup, 42 percent of bachelor's degree students have given at least a fair amount of thought to changing their major because of AI. Among associate degree students, that figure rises to 56 percent. Sixteen percent of currently enrolled students have already made the switch.

The anxiety is not abstract. At a University of Central Florida commencement ceremony earlier this year, the Class of 2026 audibly booed when a speaker called AI "the next Industrial Revolution." Similar reactions were reported at other ceremonies across the country.

The Skills That Survive Automation

The emerging consensus among educators and employers is that the most durable skills are not technical but cognitive and interpersonal. The OECD's Andreas Schleicher, who leads global education policy, has argued for years that schools still teach children to think like machines — focusing on tasks that are easy to test but also easy to automate.

"The advent of AI should push us to think harder of what makes us human. If we are not careful, we will be educating second-class robots and not first-class humans."

— Andreas Schleicher, Head of Education, OECD

Timothy Knowles, president of the Carnegie Endowment for the Advancement of Teaching, put it more directly: "Skills like critical thinking, communication, and collaboration will matter more than ever. They are literally the skills that machines can't replace."

Joseph Fuller of Harvard Business School has called for a wholesale rethinking of college curricula. "Personally, I think this looks like fewer highly specialized courses, even things like BC Calculus, and more courses that teach students how to think, reason, problem-solve, and work with data," he wrote. "Statistics. Logic. Rhetoric. Theories of mind."

What the Data Says About the Workforce

The labor market is already responding to AI in ways that complicate simplistic narratives about job destruction. A YouGov survey of 1,250 U.S. workers commissioned by sociologist researchers in August 2026 found that only about 3 percent had lost a job due to AI since 2023, while roughly 6 percent landed a role that did not exist before AI.

But the composition of the workforce is shifting. Visier's analysis of 3.6 million employment records, released in August 2026, found that overall hiring rates dropped 24 percent, even as roles in data, analytics, and AI engineering grew. Companies are now favoring experienced workers aged 35 to 50 over younger talent in some cases — a reversal of long-standing patterns.

Mercer's 2026 global survey found that only 44 percent of employees described themselves as "thriving," down from 66 percent in 2024. More than a third said they would consider quitting if left behind on AI tools.

What Parents and Students Can Do Now

For diaspora parents navigating educational choices for their children, the implications are significant. The traditional emphasis on STEM subjects and professional degrees remains relevant, but the competitive edge increasingly lies in capabilities that standardized testing does not measure: the ability to frame problems, communicate across disciplines, and adapt when the rules change.

A national survey by the American Association of Colleges and Universities and Elon University found that 95 percent of faculty believe AI will increase students' overreliance on the technology, and 90 percent said it will diminish critical thinking. Meanwhile, a Handshake survey of college seniors found that 58 percent believe they need a deep understanding of AI to succeed at work, but only 28 percent said AI was meaningfully integrated into their degree program.

"Students are telling us they want AI woven into how they actually learn, and institutions are responding with policies and occasional workshops that go nowhere near that."

— Tawnya Means, Inspire Higher Ed

The gap between what students need and what institutions offer is where the real disruption lies. Education experts suggest that rather than chasing the "perfect" AI-proof major, students should focus on building a foundation of skills that transfers across fields: mathematical reasoning, clear communication, comfort with ambiguity, and the discipline to learn continuously.

As the OECD's Schleicher has noted, the age of AI rewards not just those who know everything, but those who are willing to keep learning.
